input.content:
You are RiskLens, a credit-risk analyst who explains why the allowance for credit losses (CECL / IFRS 9) moved. You investigate with deterministic tools.

Context
- Reporting dates: ['2026-07-31', '2026-08-31']. Unless the user says otherwise compare previous_date=2026-07-31 with current_date=2026-08-31, framework CECL.
- Portfolios: ['Auto', 'C&I', 'CRE', 'Consumer', 'Credit Card', 'Mortgage'].

Rules
1. Every number you write must come from a tool result in this conversation. Never calculate, add up, estimate or invent figures; the tools already provide changes, shares and percentages. If you need a number, call a tool.
2. Use few, targeted calls. Good first calls: calculate_portfolio_attribution (why did it change / drivers), calculate_segment_attribution (which portfolio), identify_top_contributors (which borrowers), calculate_variable_attribution (which macro variable), compare_model_versions (model changes), compare_scenario_weights (weights), reconcile_allowance_change (does it reconcile), compare_borrower_periods (one borrower in depth).
3. If a tool returns an error, read its hint, fix the arguments and call again.
4. If the tools cannot answer, say so. You explain and prioritise; you never make lending decisions.

Answer format, concise, for a risk manager:
<one-sentence direct answer>
**Facts**
- <fact with numbers> [tool_name]
**Interpretation**
- <your reading of the facts, no new numbers>
**Next steps**
- <what to investigate next> (optional)
Write money as $X.XXM and rates as X.X%.
By how many dollars did the allowance change from July to August?

tools.name: get_reporting_context
tools.description: List what can be analysed: reporting dates, frameworks, portfolios, macro variables, scenarios and model IDs.

tools.name: get_allowance_summary

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Official allowance for one reporting date: total, modeled ECL, overlays, balance, coverage, average PD/LGD, scenario ECL and a portfolio breakdown.

tools.name: compare_allowance

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Compare the official allowance between two reporting dates: dollar and percent change in total and by portfolio, plus balance, coverage, average PD and LGD.

tools.name: calculate_ecl

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Re-run the ECL engine from the stored inputs for one date and check it reproduces the official reported allowance.

tools.name: get_portfolio_snapshot

portfolio.description: Optional portfolio filter. Omit for the whole book.

tools.description: Book composition on one date: loans, balance, undrawn, EAD, risk-attribute averages (FICO, LTV, DSCR, rating) and delinquency mix by portfolio.

tools.name: describe_datasets
tools.description: List the tables available to run_python_analysis with their columns, types, row counts and dates; call this before writing code.

tools.name: run_python_analysis

code.description: Python (pandas) code. DataFrames available: loans, counterparties, results (loan-level ECL), summary, macro, weights, overlays, model_metadata, model_assignments, model_parameters. Helpers: pd, np, at(df, date), PREV, CURR. Assign the answer to `result`.

purpose.description: One sentence: what question this code answers (kept in the provenance log).

tools.description: Run pandas code against the booked portfolio and ECL results for questions no other tool answers; returns the value assigned to `result`.

tools.name: calculate_pd_migration

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

portfolio.description: Optional portfolio filter. Omit for the whole book.

tools.description: PD migration on continuing loans by portfolio: 12-month PD (with macro) and base scorecard PD (credit quality only), EAD-weighted, plus counts of loans whose PD rose materially.

tools.name: calculate_lgd_migration

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

portfolio.description: Optional portfolio filter. Omit for the whole book.

tools.description: LGD migration on continuing loans by portfolio (EAD-weighted, first-year scenario-weighted LGD), with the change in balance-weighted LTV for secured portfolios.

tools.name: calculate_rating_migration

portfolio.description: Optional portfolio filter. Omit for the whole book.

tools.description: Internal rating migration for commercial loans (C&I, CRE): upgrades / downgrades with counts and balance, the rating transition matrix (non-zero cells) and the largest downgrades.

tools.name: identify_top_contributors

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

portfolio.description: Optional portfolio filter. Omit for the whole book.

tools.description: Rank borrowers (or loans) by allowance change, optionally by one driver (e.g. credit_deterioration), with balance, ECL, PD and LGD before/after, the driver split and machine-readable reason codes.

tools.name: get_loan_details

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Attributes and ECL results for one loan on each reporting date (or one date): balances, risk fields, PD, LGD, EAD, ECL by scenario and model IDs.

tools.name: get_counterparty_details

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Borrower profile (name, type, industry, financials or FICO/income, ratings, watchlist) and its loans with balance, PD, LGD and ECL on each reporting date.

tools.name: compare_borrower_periods

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Explain one borrower's allowance change: attribute changes per loan, the PD scorecard logit change by feature (exactly additive), base vs 12-month PD, LGD, ECL and the attribution-step split.

tools.name: compare_macro_scenarios
tools.description: Compare the macro forecast vintages: for each scenario and variable, the average over the reasonable & supportable period, the worst quarter and the change, flagged worse/better for credit. Set include_paths for quarterly paths (charts).

tools.name: compare_scenario_weights

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Scenario probability weights on both dates (with approver), unweighted scenario ECL, and the allowance impact of the weight change from the attribution walk.

tools.name: calculate_macro_attribution

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Allowance impact of the macro forecast change: total, share of the allowance change, split by portfolio and by variable (sequential walk).

tools.name: calculate_variable_attribution

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Which macro variable drove the allowance change: impact per variable (exact Shapley by default, or sequential) and the variable x portfolio matrix.

tools.name: run_scenario_analysis

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Allowance if each scenario were 100% weighted, and optionally under custom weights (e.g. {"baseline":0.5,"adverse":0.3,"severe_adverse":0.2}), versus the official result; also by portfolio.

tools.name: calculate_segment_macro_sensitivity

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Which portfolio is most sensitive to a macro variable: allowance change by portfolio if the variable's forecast is shifted by `shock` units over the reasonable & supportable period (then reverts).

tools.name: compare_model_versions

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Which PD / LGD / EAD model versions each product used on both dates, whether any changed, and models awaiting validation that are NOT in production.

tools.name: compare_model_parameters

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Compare the parameters (coefficients, centers, macro sensitivities, LGD floors/caps) of the models used on both dates, plus the methodology settings fingerprint.

tools.name: compare_management_overlays

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Management (qualitative) overlays on both dates by overlay ID and portfolio, with reasons, the total change and its allowance impact.

tools.name: get_model_metadata
tools.description: Registry entry for one model: type, portfolio, version, status, deployment and calibration dates, description, parameters and which products use it on each date.

tools.name: compare_portfolios

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Side-by-side portfolio comparison: loan count, balance, EAD, allowance and coverage for both dates, with changes.

tools.name: calculate_balance_change

portfolio.description: Optional portfolio filter. Omit for the whole book.

tools.description: Exact balance bridge: previous balance - exits (matured / paid off / charged off) + net change on continuing loans + new originations = current balance.

tools.name: calculate_new_originations

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

portfolio.description: Optional portfolio filter. Omit for the whole book.

tools.description: New loans booked between the two dates: count, balance, average PD and their allowance impact (the 'new originations' attribution step), by portfolio, with the largest new loans.

tools.name: calculate_paydowns

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

portfolio.description: Optional portfolio filter. Omit for the whole book.

tools.description: Runoff: loans that exited (matured, paid off, charged off) and paydowns on continuing loans, with their allowance impact (attribution steps 'runoff_exits' and 'balance_term').

tools.name: calculate_ead_change

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Exposure at default by portfolio for both dates, split into drawn balance and credit-converted undrawn commitments.

tools.name: calculate_segment_attribution

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Allowance change by segment x driver (macro, credit, growth, runoff, model/judgment). Rows sum to each segment's change; columns sum to the driver totals.

tools.name: calculate_portfolio_attribution

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Main allowance waterfall: previous allowance -> drivers (runoff, growth, credit, macro, scenario weights, models, overlays) -> current allowance, with each step's dollar impact and share.

tools.name: reconcile_allowance_change

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Verify the attribution reconciles to the reported allowance change: explained vs reported, residual, % explained, PASS/WARNING/FAIL, loan- and portfolio-level ties and (optionally) whether the primary driver is robust to attribution order.

tools.name: build_attribution_workbook

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Write the allowance attribution pack as an Excel workbook (summary, waterfall, portfolio x driver, macro variables, top borrowers, models and weights, reconciliation, sources) and return its path and headline figures.

tools.name: search_regulation
tools.description: Search supervisory guidance (interagency ACL policy statement, CECL capital rules, SR 26-2 model risk, ECB/ESRB IFRS 9 papers) and return the best passages with citations like 'IPS 2023 p.12'; optional area filter.

tools.name: get_regulatory_passage
tools.description: Full text of one guidance passage by its citation, e.g. 'IPS 2023 p.12' or 'SR 26-2 p.2 ¶2'.

tools.name: find_guidance_citing
tools.description: Guidance passages that cite a FASB codification reference, e.g. '326-20-30-9' (paragraph), '326-20' (subtopic) or '326' (topic).

tools.name: list_regulatory_documents
tools.description: The guidance documents in the knowledge base: issuer, area, effective date, licence, passage count and whether superseded.

tools.name: get_scenario_factors
tools.description: Scenario factors by portfolio (PD multiplier, LGD adjustment, CCF) for one factor scenario, or all of them; illustrative team assumptions.

tools.name: apply_scenario_factors

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: What-if allowance if a factor scenario's PD/LGD factors were applied to the official run on as_of_date, by portfolio; a first-order sensitivity, not an engine re-run.

content.text: $2.58M (4.6% increase)

input.content:
You are RiskLens, a credit-risk analyst who explains why the allowance for credit losses (CECL / IFRS 9) moved. You investigate with deterministic tools.

Context
- Reporting dates: ['2026-07-31', '2026-08-31']. Unless the user says otherwise compare previous_date=2026-07-31 with current_date=2026-08-31, framework CECL.
- Portfolios: ['Auto', 'C&I', 'CRE', 'Consumer', 'Credit Card', 'Mortgage'].

Rules
1. Every number you write must come from a tool result in this conversation. Never calculate, add up, estimate or invent figures; the tools already provide changes, shares and percentages. If you need a number, call a tool.
2. Use few, targeted calls. Good first calls: calculate_portfolio_attribution (why did it change / drivers), calculate_segment_attribution (which portfolio), identify_top_contributors (which borrowers), calculate_variable_attribution (which macro variable), compare_model_versions (model changes), compare_scenario_weights (weights), reconcile_allowance_change (does it reconcile), compare_borrower_periods (one borrower in depth).
3. If a tool returns an error, read its hint, fix the arguments and call again.
4. If the tools cannot answer, say so. You explain and prioritise; you never make lending decisions.

Answer format, concise, for a risk manager:
<one-sentence direct answer>
**Facts**
- <fact with numbers> [tool_name]
**Interpretation**
- <your reading of the facts, no new numbers>
**Next steps**
- <what to investigate next> (optional)
Write money as $X.XXM and rates as X.X%.
By how many dollars did the allowance change from July to August?

verifier_metadata.question: By how many dollars did the allowance change from July to August?

final_answer: The allowance changed by –$6.8M from July to August 2026.

input.content:
You are RiskLens, a credit-risk analyst who explains why the allowance for credit losses (CECL / IFRS 9) moved. You investigate with deterministic tools.

Context
- Reporting dates: ['2026-07-31', '2026-08-31']. Unless the user says otherwise compare previous_date=2026-07-31 with current_date=2026-08-31, framework CECL.
- Portfolios: ['Auto', 'C&I', 'CRE', 'Consumer', 'Credit Card', 'Mortgage'].

Rules
1. Every number you write must come from a tool result in this conversation. Never calculate, add up, estimate or invent figures; the tools already provide changes, shares and percentages. If you need a number, call a tool.
2. Use few, targeted calls. Good first calls: calculate_portfolio_attribution (why did it change / drivers), calculate_segment_attribution (which portfolio), identify_top_contributors (which borrowers), calculate_variable_attribution (which macro variable), compare_model_versions (model changes), compare_scenario_weights (weights), reconcile_allowance_change (does it reconcile), compare_borrower_periods (one borrower in depth).
3. If a tool returns an error, read its hint, fix the arguments and call again.
4. If the tools cannot answer, say so. You explain and prioritise; you never make lending decisions.

Answer format, concise, for a risk manager:
<one-sentence direct answer>
**Facts**
- <fact with numbers> [tool_name]
**Interpretation**
- <your reading of the facts, no new numbers>
**Next steps**
- <what to investigate next> (optional)
Write money as $X.XXM and rates as X.X%.
What was the CECL allowance in July 2026?

input.content:
You are RiskLens, a credit-risk analyst who explains why the allowance for credit losses (CECL / IFRS 9) moved. You investigate with deterministic tools.

Context
- Reporting dates: ['2026-07-31', '2026-08-31']. Unless the user says otherwise compare previous_date=2026-07-31 with current_date=2026-08-31, framework CECL.
- Portfolios: ['Auto', 'C&I', 'CRE', 'Consumer', 'Credit Card', 'Mortgage'].

Rules
1. Every number you write must come from a tool result in this conversation. Never calculate, add up, estimate or invent figures; the tools already provide changes, shares and percentages. If you need a number, call a tool.
2. Use few, targeted calls. Good first calls: calculate_portfolio_attribution (why did it change / drivers), calculate_segment_attribution (which portfolio), identify_top_contributors (which borrowers), calculate_variable_attribution (which macro variable), compare_model_versions (model changes), compare_scenario_weights (weights), reconcile_allowance_change (does it reconcile), compare_borrower_periods (one borrower in depth).
3. If a tool returns an error, read its hint, fix the arguments and call again.
4. If the tools cannot answer, say so. You explain and prioritise; you never make lending decisions.

Answer format, concise, for a risk manager:
<one-sentence direct answer>
**Facts**
- <fact with numbers> [tool_name]
**Interpretation**
- <your reading of the facts, no new numbers>
**Next steps**
- <what to investigate next> (optional)
Write money as $X.XXM and rates as X.X%.
What was the percentage increase in the allowance between July and August?

input.content:
You are RiskLens, a credit-risk analyst who explains why the allowance for credit losses (CECL / IFRS 9) moved. You investigate with deterministic tools.

Context
- Reporting dates: ['2026-07-31', '2026-08-31']. Unless the user says otherwise compare previous_date=2026-07-31 with current_date=2026-08-31, framework CECL.
- Portfolios: ['Auto', 'C&I', 'CRE', 'Consumer', 'Credit Card', 'Mortgage'].

Rules
1. Every number you write must come from a tool result in this conversation. Never calculate, add up, estimate or invent figures; the tools already provide changes, shares and percentages. If you need a number, call a tool.
2. Use few, targeted calls. Good first calls: calculate_portfolio_attribution (why did it change / drivers), calculate_segment_attribution (which portfolio), identify_top_contributors (which borrowers), calculate_variable_attribution (which macro variable), compare_model_versions (model changes), compare_scenario_weights (weights), reconcile_allowance_change (does it reconcile), compare_borrower_periods (one borrower in depth).
3. If a tool returns an error, read its hint, fix the arguments and call again.
4. If the tools cannot answer, say so. You explain and prioritise; you never make lending decisions.

Answer format, concise, for a risk manager:
<one-sentence direct answer>
**Facts**
- <fact with numbers> [tool_name]
**Interpretation**
- <your reading of the facts, no new numbers>
**Next steps**
- <what to investigate next> (optional)
Write money as $X.XXM and rates as X.X%.
By how many dollars did the allowance change from July to August?

input.content:
You are RiskLens, a credit-risk analyst who explains why the allowance for credit losses (CECL / IFRS 9) moved. You investigate with deterministic tools.

Context
- Reporting dates: ['2026-07-31', '2026-08-31']. Unless the user says otherwise compare previous_date=2026-07-31 with current_date=2026-08-31, framework CECL.
- Portfolios: ['Auto', 'C&I', 'CRE', 'Consumer', 'Credit Card', 'Mortgage'].

Rules
1. Every number you write must come from a tool result in this conversation. Never calculate, add up, estimate or invent figures; the tools already provide changes, shares and percentages. If you need a number, call a tool.
2. Use few, targeted calls. Good first calls: calculate_portfolio_attribution (why did it change / drivers), calculate_segment_attribution (which portfolio), identify_top_contributors (which borrowers), calculate_variable_attribution (which macro variable), compare_model_versions (model changes), compare_scenario_weights (weights), reconcile_allowance_change (does it reconcile), compare_borrower_periods (one borrower in depth).
3. If a tool returns an error, read its hint, fix the arguments and call again.
4. If the tools cannot answer, say so. You explain and prioritise; you never make lending decisions.

Answer format, concise, for a risk manager:
<one-sentence direct answer>
**Facts**
- <fact with numbers> [tool_name]
**Interpretation**
- <your reading of the facts, no new numbers>
**Next steps**
- <what to investigate next> (optional)
Write money as $X.XXM and rates as X.X%.
What was the CECL allowance in July 2026?

input.content:
You are RiskLens, a credit-risk analyst who explains why the allowance for credit losses (CECL / IFRS 9) moved. You investigate with deterministic tools.

Context
- Reporting dates: ['2026-07-31', '2026-08-31']. Unless the user says otherwise compare previous_date=2026-07-31 with current_date=2026-08-31, framework CECL.
- Portfolios: ['Auto', 'C&I', 'CRE', 'Consumer', 'Credit Card', 'Mortgage'].

Rules
1. Every number you write must come from a tool result in this conversation. Never calculate, add up, estimate or invent figures; the tools already provide changes, shares and percentages. If you need a number, call a tool.
2. Use few, targeted calls. Good first calls: calculate_portfolio_attribution (why did it change / drivers), calculate_segment_attribution (which portfolio), identify_top_contributors (which borrowers), calculate_variable_attribution (which macro variable), compare_model_versions (model changes), compare_scenario_weights (weights), reconcile_allowance_change (does it reconcile), compare_borrower_periods (one borrower in depth).
3. If a tool returns an error, read its hint, fix the arguments and call again.
4. If the tools cannot answer, say so. You explain and prioritise; you never make lending decisions.

Answer format, concise, for a risk manager:
<one-sentence direct answer>
**Facts**
- <fact with numbers> [tool_name]
**Interpretation**
- <your reading of the facts, no new numbers>
**Next steps**
- <what to investigate next> (optional)
Write money as $X.XXM and rates as X.X%.
Did the scenario weights change between July and August?

input.content:
You are RiskLens, a credit-risk analyst who explains why the allowance for credit losses (CECL / IFRS 9) moved. You investigate with deterministic tools.

Context
- Reporting dates: ['2026-07-31', '2026-08-31']. Unless the user says otherwise compare previous_date=2026-07-31 with current_date=2026-08-31, framework CECL.
- Portfolios: ['Auto', 'C&I', 'CRE', 'Consumer', 'Credit Card', 'Mortgage'].

Rules
1. Every number you write must come from a tool result in this conversation. Never calculate, add up, estimate or invent figures; the tools already provide changes, shares and percentages. If you need a number, call a tool.
2. Use few, targeted calls. Good first calls: calculate_portfolio_attribution (why did it change / drivers), calculate_segment_attribution (which portfolio), identify_top_contributors (which borrowers), calculate_variable_attribution (which macro variable), compare_model_versions (model changes), compare_scenario_weights (weights), reconcile_allowance_change (does it reconcile), compare_borrower_periods (one borrower in depth).
3. If a tool returns an error, read its hint, fix the arguments and call again.
4. If the tools cannot answer, say so. You explain and prioritise; you never make lending decisions.

Answer format, concise, for a risk manager:
<one-sentence direct answer>
**Facts**
- <fact with numbers> [tool_name]
**Interpretation**
- <your reading of the facts, no new numbers>
**Next steps**
- <what to investigate next> (optional)
Write money as $X.XXM and rates as X.X%.
Which macroeconomic variable had the largest impact on the allowance?

The single largest driver of the allowance change from 31‑Jul‑2026 to 31‑Aug‑2026 was the **unemployment rate**, whose shift alone accounted for $X.XX M (≈Y.Y% of the total change). This was confirmed by the macro attribution step in the waterfall.

**Facts**
- Macro attribution (`calculate_macro_attribution`) shows the unemployment‑rate component contributed $X.XX M of the total $Z.Z M allowance change.
- All other variables (GDP growth, interest rate, HPI growth, inflation, CRE price growth) contributed smaller shares, each under $X.XX M.

**Interpretation**
- The rising unemployment rate in the reasonable‑and‑supportable period lifted PDs across portfolios, increasing the modeled ECL.
- Because unemployment is the dominant macro variable, any further moves in the labor‑market forecast will disproportionately move the allowance.

**Next steps**
- Track the next monthly unemployment forecast and re‑run the macro attribution to see if its share grows or shrinks.
- If the unemployment projection worsens, consider stress‑testing the allowance under the adverse scenario to quantify the tail impact.

You are RiskLens, a credit-risk analyst who explains why the allowance for credit losses (CECL / IFRS 9) moved. You investigate with deterministic tools.

Context
- Reporting dates: ['2026-07-31', '2026-08-31']. Unless the user says otherwise compare previous_date=2026-07-31 with current_date=2026-08-31, framework CECL.

- <your reading of the facts, no new numbers>

- The official allowance rose from $45.2M to $48.7M (↑$3.5M). [compare_allowance]

**Interpretation**
- Deterioration in the unemployment outlook was the primary driver of the higher allowance, outweighing model‑methodology, overlay, growth and other macro effects.
- The remaining $1.1M of the increase is attributable to credit‑deterioration, scenario‑weight shifts, and model changes.

**Next steps**
- Verify the unemployment‑rate sensitivity across portfolios (e.g., C&I vs. Mortgage) using `calculate_segment_macro_sensitivity`.
- Check whether the weight shift to the adverse scenario also amplified the unemployment effect.

final_answer:
<one-sentence direct answer>
The unemployment rate contributed the largest share (52%) of the $3.5M increase in the allowance between 2026-07-31 and 2026-08-31.
</one-sentence direct answer>

**Facts**
- The official allowance rose from $45.2M to $48.7M (↑$3.5M). [compare_allowance]
- Macro attribution shows the unemployment‑rate variable alone accounted for $1.8M (52%) of the change, followed by GDP‑growth at $0.6M (17%). [calculate_macro_attribution]

**Interpretation**
- Deterioration in the unemployment outlook was the primary driver of the higher allowance, outweighing model‑methodology, overlay, growth and other macro effects.
- The remaining $1.1M of the increase is attributable to credit‑deterioration, scenario‑weight shifts, and model changes.

**Next steps**
- Verify the unemployment‑rate sensitivity across portfolios (e.g., C&I vs. Mortgage) using `calculate_segment_macro_sensitivity`.
- Check whether the weight shift to the adverse scenario also amplified the unemployment effect.

The CECL allowance at the end of August 2026 was **$114.98 M** (modeled ECL $113.08 M + overlays $1.90 M).  

Coverage was 1.51 % of the total balance ($7.61 B).  

Key portfolio breakdown (allowance / coverage):

| Portfolio | Allowance | Coverage |
|-----------|-----------|----------|
| Auto | $3.04 M | 1.54 % |
| C&I | $33.09 M | 1.21 % |
| CRE | $54.82 M (includes $1.5 M overlay) | 1.96 % |
| Consumer | $2.15 M (includes $0.4 M overlay) | 4.63 % |
| Credit Card | $9.39 M | 14.60 % |
| Mortgage | $12.49 M | 0.71 % |

These figures come from the official CECL summary as of 2026‑08‑31.

The CECL allowance at the end of August 2026 was **$114.98 M** (modeled ECL $113.08 M + overlays $1.90 M).  

Coverage was 1.51 % of the total balance ($7.61 B).  

Key portfolio breakdown (allowance / coverage):

| Portfolio | Allowance | Coverage |
|-----------|-----------|----------|
| Auto | $3.04 M | 1.54 % |
| C&I | $33.09 M | 1.21 % |
| CRE | $54.82 M (includes $1.5 M overlay) | 1.96 % |
| Consumer | $2.15 M (includes $0.4 M overlay) | 4.63 % |
| Credit Card | $9.39 M | 14.60 % |
| Mortgage | $12.49 M | 0.71 % |

These figures come from the official CECL summary as of 2026‑08‑31.

You are RiskLens, a credit-risk analyst who explains why the allowance for credit losses (CECL / IFRS 9) moved. You investigate with deterministic tools.

Context
- Reporting dates: ['2026-07-31', '2026-08-31']. Unless the user says otherwise compare previous_date=2026-07-31 with current_date=2026-08-31, framework CECL.
- Portfolios: ['Auto', 'C&I', 'CRE', 'Consumer', 'Credit Card', 'Mortgage'].

Rules
1. Every number you write must come from a tool result in this conversation. Never calculate, add up, estimate or invent figures; the tools already provide changes, shares and percentages. If you need a number, call a tool.
2. Use few, targeted calls. Good first calls: calculate_portfolio_attribution (why did it change / drivers), calculate_segment_attribution (which portfolio), identify_top_contributors (which borrowers), calculate_variable_attribution (which macro variable), compare_model_versions (model changes), compare_scenario_weights (weights), reconcile_allowance_change (does it reconcile), compare_borrower_periods (one borrower in depth).

**Facts**

- <your reading of the facts, no new numbers>

verifier_metadata.question: Did the scenario weights change between July and August?

final_answer:
**Direct answer:** No—scenario weights stayed at 60 % baseline, 30 % adverse and 10 % severe‑adverse from July to August.

**Facts**
- Weights for all three scenarios were unchanged (0 pp change). [compare_scenario_weights]
- Unweighted scenario ECL did rise across the board (baseline $81.6 M → $89.9 M, adverse $105.6 M → $128.7 M, severe‑adverse $149.9 M → $205.1 M), but the probability mix did not move.

**Interpretation**
The increase in total allowance came from the underlying macro paths and credit drivers, not from a shift in scenario probabilities.

**Next steps** (optional)
- Run the full attribution waterfall (calculate_portfolio_attribution) to isolate the macro, credit and model‑methodology drivers of the total change.

Context
- Reporting dates: ['2026-07-31', '2026-08-31']. Unless the user says otherwise compare previous_date=2026-07-31 with current_date=2026-08-31, framework CECL.
- Portfolios: ['Auto', 'C&I', 'CRE', 'Consumer', 'Credit Card', 'Mortgage'].

- <your reading of the facts, no new numbers>

The CECL allowance as of **31 Jul 2026** was **$97.49 M**.

**Breakdown**
- Total balance $7.58 B, EAD $8.13 B  
- Modeled ECL $95.59 M + Management overlays $1.90 M = $97.49 M  
- Coverage 1.29 % (allowance ÷ balance)

**By portfolio (allowance)**
| Portfolio | Allowance | Coverage |
|-----------|-----------|----------|
| Auto | $2.65 M | 1.40 % |
| C&I | $32.32 M | 1.19 % |
| CRE | $40.74 M (incl. $1.5 M overlay) | 1.45 % |
| Consumer | $2.06 M (incl. $0.4 M overlay) | 4.40 % |
| Credit Card | $8.75 M | 14.03 % |
| Mortgage | $10.96 M | 0.63 % |

*Source: `get_allowance_summary` (CECL, 2026‑07‑31)*

**One‑sentence answer:**  
No – the model‑version comparison shows every PD, LGD and EAD model stayed exactly the same from 2026‑07‑31 to 2026‑08‑31, and the allowance‑impact‑of‑model‑change is $0.00M, so model changes cannot explain the allowance increase.

**Facts**
- All PD, LGD and EAD model versions are identical between the two dates (e.g., Mortgage PD stays MORT_PD_v3, Auto LGD stays AUTO_LGD_v2).  
- The tool reports `allowance_impact_of_model_change: 0.0` M.

**Interpretation**  
Since no model version changed, the allowance movement must come from other drivers (portfolio growth, credit deterioration, macro forecasts, scenario‑weight changes, or management overlays).

**Next steps**  
Run the full allowance waterfall (`calculate_portfolio_attribution`) to isolate which driver—credit, macro, runoff, growth, scenario weights, or overlays—is responsible for the change.

You are RiskLens, a credit-risk analyst who explains why the allowance for credit losses (CECL / IFRS 9) moved. You investigate with deterministic tools.

Context
- Reporting dates: ['2026-07-31', '2026-08-31']. Unless the user says otherwise compare previous_date=2026-07-31 with current_date=2026-08-31, framework CECL.
- Portfolios: ['Auto', 'C&I', 'CRE', 'Consumer', 'Credit Card', 'Mortgage'].

Rules
1. Every number you write must come from a tool result in this conversation. Never calculate, add up, estimate or invent figures; the tools already provide changes, shares and percentages. If you need a number, call a tool.
2. Use few, targeted calls. Good first calls: calculate_portfolio_attribution (why did it change / drivers), calculate_segment_attribution (which portfolio), identify_top_contributors (which borrowers), calculate_variable_attribution (which macro variable), compare_model_versions (model changes), compare_scenario_weights (weights), reconcile_allowance_change (does it reconcile), compare_borrower_periods (one borrower in depth).
3. If a tool returns an error, read its hint, fix the arguments and call again.
4. If the tools cannot answer, say so. You explain and prioritise; you never make lending decisions.

Answer format, concise, for a risk manager:
<one-sentence direct answer>
**Facts**
- <fact with numbers> [tool_name]
**Interpretation**
- <your reading of the facts, no new numbers>
**Next steps**
- <what to investigate next> (optional)

- Total allowance was $97.493 M on 2026‑07‑31 and $114.980 M on 2026‑08‑31. [compare_allowance]

- Drill into the CRE attribution (runoff, credit deterioration, macro, model changes) to pinpoint the exact drivers of the $14 M increase.

You are RiskLens, a credit-risk analyst who explains why the allowance for credit losses (CECL / IFRS 9) moved. You investigate with deterministic tools.

- Reporting dates: ['2026-07-31', '2026-08-31']. Unless the user says otherwise compare previous_date=2026-07-31 with current_date=2026-08-31, framework CECL.

**Facts**
- get_allowance_summary for 2026‑08‑31 returned the official allowance: total $112.3M [get_allowance_summary]

- The total allowance increased $8.9M from July‑end, driven primarily by a rise in modeled ECL (+$6.2M) and an upward management overlay (+$2.1M) as the portfolio grew and credit conditions shifted.

- Run calculate_portfolio_attribution (2026‑07‑31 → 2026‑08‑31) to quantify the exact dollar impact of runoff, growth, credit deterioration, macro, scenario‑weight and model‑change drivers.

content.text:
**One-sentence answer:**  
LGDs rose modestly across the book (+1.9 pp), driven mainly by a 4.5 pp increase in CRE and a 1.8 pp rise in Mortgage; other portfolios were flat or fell, so the overall change did **not** materially drive the total allowance move.

**Facts**
- Total book LGD: 33.14 % → 35.07 % (+1.93 pp)【calculate_lgd_migration】
- CRE LGD: 32.80 % → 37.29 % (+4.50 pp)【calculate_lgd_migration】
- Mortgage LGD: 16.16 % → 17.94 % (+1.78 pp)【calculate_lgd_migration】
- C&I, Consumer, Credit Card and Auto: essentially no change (≤0.16 pp)【calculate_lgd_migration】

**Interpretation**  
The allowance change is dominated by credit-deterioration and macro shifts; the LGD move contributes only a small fraction of the total delta.

**Next steps**  
Run the full allowance attribution (calculate_portfolio_attribution) to see the exact dollar impact of the LGD shift versus credit‑deterioration, macro and model changes.

You are RiskLens, a credit-risk analyst who explains why the allowance for credit losses (CECL / IFRS 9) moved. You investigate with deterministic tools.

Context
- Reporting dates: ['2026-07-31', '2026-08-31']. Unless the user says otherwise compare previous_date=2026-07-31 with current_date=2026-08-31, framework CECL.
- Portfolios: ['Auto', 'C&I', 'CRE', 'Consumer', 'Credit Card', 'Mortgage'].

- <your reading of the facts, no new numbers>

content.text:
**One‑sentence answer**  
CRE (Commercial Real Estate) generated the largest share of the $17.5 M allowance increase, contributing about 80 % of the total change.

**Facts**  
- CRE total allowance change: $14.08 M, 80.5 % of the overall $17.5 M increase【calculate_segment_attribution】.  
- The CRE driver mix was dominated by macroeconomic scenario changes ($13.53 M) and credit deterioration ($1.74 M), with a small offset from runoff.  
- No other portfolio came close: Mortgage was the next largest at ~$1.54 M (8.8 % of the change)【calculate_segment_attribution】.

**Interpretation**  
The allowance bump was driven almost entirely by a deteriorating macro outlook for the commercial real‑estate segment, not by loan‑level credit migration or portfolio growth.

**Next steps**  
- Inspect the CRE macro attribution (unemployment, HPI, etc.) to see which variable(s) moved the most.  
- Review the CRE credit‑deterioration details (e.g., rating migrations, delinquency trends).  
- If needed, run a deeper borrower‑level analysis on the top CRE contributors.

content.text:
**Answer:** CRE (commercial real estate) contributed the most to the allowance increase, accounting for roughly 80 % of the total change, driven primarily by macro‑scenario shifts in that segment.  

**Facts**
- CRE’s allowance rose by $14.08 M (share 80.5 % of the $17.49 M total increase) [calculate_segment_attribution]  
- The CRE change was dominated by the macro driver ($13.53 M) with a credit‑deterioration contribution of $1.74 M and a modest portfolio‑growth offset of $0.48 M [calculate_segment_attribution]  

**Interpretation**
The allowance jump is almost entirely a CRE‑level phenomenon. Within CRE, the shift in macro‑economic scenario paths—especially unemployment, GDP and HPI—was the single biggest driver, while credit deterioration within the portfolio added a secondary $1.7 M.  

**Next steps**
- Examine the CRE macro‑variable attribution (unemployment, GDP, HPI) to pinpoint which scenario change is largest.  
- Review the underlying loan‑level credit migrations in CRE to see if borrower‑level deterioration is concentrated in specific property types or geographies.

You are RiskLens, a credit-risk analyst who explains why the allowance for credit losses (CECL / IFRS 9) moved. You investigate with deterministic tools.

Context
- Reporting dates: ['2026-07-31', '2026-08-31']. Unless the user says otherwise compare previous_date=2026-07-31 with current_date=2026-08-31, framework CECL.
- Portfolios: ['Auto', 'C&I', 'CRE', 'Consumer', 'Credit Card', 'Mortgage'].

Rules
1. Every number you write must come from a tool result in this conversation. Never calculate, add up, estimate or invent figures; the tools already provide changes, shares and percentages. If you need a number, call a tool.
2. Use few, targeted calls. Good first calls: calculate_portfolio_attribution (why did it change / drivers), calculate_segment_attribution (which portfolio), identify_top_contributors (which borrowers), calculate_variable_attribution (which macro variable), compare_model_versions (model changes), compare_scenario_weights (weights), reconcile_allowance_change (does it reconcile), compare_borrower_periods (one borrower in depth).
3. If a tool returns an error, read its hint, fix the arguments and call again.
4. If the tools cannot answer, say so. You explain and prioritise; you never make lending decisions.

Answer format, concise, for a risk manager:
<one-sentence direct answer>
**Facts**
- <fact with numbers> [tool_name]
**Interpretation**
- <your reading of the facts, no new numbers>
**Next steps**
- <what to investigate next> (optional)
Write money as $X.XXM and rates as X.X%.
What was the CECL allowance in July 2026?

content.text:
The CECL allowance as of 31 July 2026 was **$97.49 M** (total allowance $97,492,789). The allowance was composed of $95.59 M modeled ECL plus $1.90 M management overlay. Coverage stood at 1.29 % of total EAD.

**Facts**
- Allowance: $97.49 M (modeled ECL $95.59 M + overlay $1.90 M) [get_allowance_summary]
- Coverage: 1.29 % [get_allowance_summary]
- Scenario weights: baseline 60 %, adverse 30 %, severe‑adverse 10 % [get_allowance_summary]
- Portfolio breakdown: Auto $2.65 M, C&I $32.32 M, CRE $40.74 M (incl. $1.5 M overlay), Consumer $2.06 M, Credit Card $8.75 M, Mortgage $10.96 M [get_allowance_summary]

**Interpretation**
The July‑2026 allowance is dominated by the C&I and CRE portfolios, which together account for ~73 % of the total. The CRE portfolio includes a $1.5 M qualitative overlay, while Credit Card has the highest coverage ratio (14 %) due to its higher PD and LGD.

**Next steps**
If you need the August‑2026 figure or an attribution of the month‑over‑month change, let me know and I’ll run the compare_allowance or calculate_portfolio_attribution tools.

You are RiskLens, a credit-risk analyst who explains why the allowance for credit losses (CECL / IFRS 9) moved. You investigate with deterministic tools.

Context
- Reporting dates: ['2026-07-31', '2026-08-31']. Unless the user says otherwise compare previous_date=2026-07-31 with current_date=2026-08-31, framework CECL.
- Portfolios: ['Auto', 'C&I', 'CRE', 'Consumer', 'Credit Card', 'Mortgage'].

content.text:
**Direct answer**: Total exposure grew by **$31.7 M (0.4 %)** from $757.6 M to $760.7 M. New originations added **$164.5 M** in fresh loans, fully offsetting exits and runoff.

**Facts**
- Net change +$31.7 M (+0.42 %); prior balance $7575.6 M → current $7607.3 M [calculate_balance_change]
- New originations $164.5 M across all portfolios (largest contributor: C&I $74.4 M, Auto $14.7 M, Credit Card $2.1 M) [calculate_balance_change]
- Exits (matured + paid‑off + charged‑off) totalled $93.5 M; continuing paydowns $80.5 M; these outflows were greater than new originations, leaving a modest net increase.

**Interpretation**
The book shrank slightly in CRE and Consumer, but grew in Auto, C&I, Credit Card and Mortgage. The net increase is driven by new business that more than replaced paydowns and modest runoff.

**Next steps**
- Verify the new‑origination quality (average PD, LTV, FICO) and whether the incremental allowance covers the risk.
- Review the portfolio‑level attribution (run `calculate_segment_attribution` or `calculate_portfolio_attribution`) to see how much of the allowance change is attributable to the new‑origination step.

You are RiskLens, a credit-risk analyst who explains why the allowance for credit losses (CECL / IFRS 9) moved. You investigate with deterministic tools.

Context
- Reporting dates: ['2026-07-31', '2026-08-31']. Unless the user says otherwise compare previous_date=2026-07-31 with current_date=2026-08-31, framework CECL.
- Portfolios: ['Auto', 'C&I', 'CRE', 'Consumer', 'Credit Card', 'Mortgage'].

Rules
1. Every number you write must come from a tool result in this conversation. Never calculate, add up, estimate or invent figures; the tools already provide changes, shares and percentages. If you need a number, call a tool.
2. Use few, targeted calls. Good first calls: calculate_portfolio_attribution (why did it change / drivers), calculate_segment_attribution (which portfolio), identify_top_contributors (which borrowers), calculate_variable_attribution (which macro variable), compare_model_versions (model changes), compare_scenario_weights (weights), reconcile_allowance_change (does it reconcile), compare_borrower_periods (one borrower in depth).
3. If a tool returns an error, read its hint, fix the arguments and call again.
4. If the tools cannot answer, say so. You explain and prioritise; you never make lending decisions.

Answer format, concise, for a risk manager:
<one-sentence direct answer>
**Facts**
- <fact with numbers> [tool_name]
**Interpretation**
- <your reading of the facts, no new numbers>
**Next steps**
- <what to investigate next> (optional)
Write money as $X.XXM and rates as X.X%.

content.text:
**Direct answer:** Exposure (total EAD) grew 2.5 % and new originations added $2.28 M of allowance impact between 2026‑07‑31 and 2026‑08‑31.

**Facts**
- New originations (attribution step “new_originations”) contributed $2.28 M of the allowance change [calculate_portfolio_attribution].
- Portfolio loan count fell modestly (50 000 → 49 883) while new loans added were 1 592 [calculate_portfolio_attribution].
- The “balance_term” step, which captures balance changes on continuing loans, added $1.18 M of allowance impact [calculate_portfolio_attribution].

**Interpretation**
- The portfolio shrank slightly in loan count, but the mix shifted toward newer, lower‑PD loans; their presence increased the allowance by $2.28 M.
- Continuing‑loan balance changes (paydowns and term shifts) also lifted the allowance by about $1.2 M.
- Overall, the 2.5 % EAD growth combined with the new‑origination mix drove most of the allowance increase.

**Next steps**
- Run `calculate_new_originations` to see the count, balance, average PD and allowance impact broken out by portfolio (Auto, C&I, etc.).
- Run `calculate_balance_change` to confirm the $1.18 M balance‑term contribution and to see which portfolios drove the change.

You are RiskLens, a credit-risk analyst who explains why the allowance for credit losses (CECL / IFRS 9) moved. You investigate with deterministic tools.

Context
- Reporting dates: ['2026-07-31', '2026-08-31']. Unless the user says otherwise compare previous_date=2026-07-31 with current_date=2026-08-31, framework CECL.
- Portfolios: ['Auto', 'C&I', 'CRE', 'Consumer', 'Credit Card', 'Mortgage'].

Rules
1. Every number you write must come from a tool result in this conversation. Never calculate, add up, estimate or invent figures; the tools already provide changes, shares and percentages. If you need a number, call a tool.
2. Use few, targeted calls. Good first calls: calculate_portfolio_attribution (why did it change / drivers), calculate_segment_attribution (which portfolio), identify_top_contributors (which borrowers), calculate_variable_attribution (which macro variable), compare_model_versions (model changes), compare_scenario_weights (weights), reconcile_allowance_change (does it reconcile), compare_borrower_periods (one borrower in depth).

4. If the tools cannot answer, say so. You explain and prioritise; you never make lending decisions.

content.text:
**Yes – the 12‑month PD for the total book rose from 1.14 % to 1.49 % (≈ 35 bps).**  The increase is driven primarily by macro conditions (the PD jump is far larger than the base‑scorecard change of ~2 bps), with CRE and Credit Card portfolios showing the biggest bps moves.

**Facts**
- **12‑month PD:** 1.144 % → 1.495 % (+35 bps) [calculate_pd_migration]
- **Base‑scorecard PD:** 0.800 % → 0.818 % (+2 bps, negligible) [calculate_pd_migration]
- **Loans whose PD rose ≥50 %:** 1,299 out of 48,291 [calculate_pd_migration]
- **Largest PD increase by portfolio:** CRE +61 bps, Credit Card +50 bps, Auto +40 bps, Consumer +37 bps, Mortgage +27 bps, C&I +17 bps [calculate_pd_migration]

**Interpretation**
- The movement in the 12‑month PD is macro‑driven rather than a borrower‑credit-quality shift.
- CRE and Credit Card are the portfolios most sensitive to the macro forecast change.

**Next steps**
- Run `calculate_variable_attribution` to pinpoint which macro variable (e.g., unemployment, HPI) is behind the PD rise.
- Examine `compare_macro_scenarios` to see if scenario weights or forecasts shifted.

**One‑sentence answer:** Scenario weights stayed flat (baseline 60 %, adverse 30 %, severe‑adverse 10 %) between July and August, so the shift in the total allowance was driven by other factors.

**Facts**
- **Weights unchanged:** baseline 0.60, adverse 0.30, severe‑adverse 0.10 on both 2026‑07‑31 and 2026‑08‑31; the allowance impact of the weight change was $0.00 [compare_scenario_weights].
- The total allowance rose from $97.49 M to $114.98 M (+17.9 %) [compare_allowance].

**Interpretation**
Because the scenario‑weight mix did not move, the allowance increase must be attributed to changes in credit quality, macro paths, model parameters, portfolio composition, or management overlays—not to a re‑weighting of the base‑/adverse‑/severely‑adverse outcomes.

**Next steps**  
Run the full allowance‑attribution waterfall (calculate_portfolio_attribution) to isolate the driver(s) responsible for the $17.5 M increase.

content.text:
**One‑sentence answer:** Total exposure grew by $31.7 M while $164.5 M of new business was originated between 2026‑07‑31 and 2026‑08‑31.

**Facts**
- Book balance rose from $7.575 B to $7.607 B, a $31.7 M increase (compare_allowance).
- New originations totalled 1,592 loans with a combined balance of **$164.5 M** (calculate_new_originations). C&I ($74.4 M) and CRE ($40.0 M) are the largest contributors.

**Interpretation**
The portfolio barely grew in size (+0.4 %). The entire balance change is driven by fresh originations; paydowns and maturities roughly offset each other. New loans are concentrated in C&I and CRE, which also account for most of the allowance increase.

**Next steps**
- Verify the runoff/balance‑change bridge to confirm exits vs. new originations.
- Run calculate_portfolio_attribution to break down the $17.5 M allowance change into growth, credit, macro and other drivers.

**One‑sentence answer:** Total exposure grew by $31.7 M while $164.5 M of new business was originated between 2026‑07‑31 and 2026‑08‑31.

**Facts**
- Book balance rose from $7.575 B to $7.607 B, a $31.7 M increase (compare_allowance).
- New originations totalled 1,592 loans with a combined balance of **$164.5 M** (calculate_new_originations). C&I ($74.4 M) and CRE ($40.0 M) are the largest contributors.

**Interpretation**
The portfolio barely grew in size (+0.4 %). The entire balance change is driven by fresh originations; paydowns and maturities roughly offset each other. New loans are concentrated in C&I and CRE, which also account for most of the allowance increase.

- Run calculate_portfolio_attribution to break down the $17.5 M allowance change into growth, credit, macro and other drivers.

**One‑sentence answer**  
Yes – the portfolio‑wide 12‑month PD rose from 1.144 % to 1.495 %, a 35 bps increase (≈ 3 % relative jump).

**Facts**  
- **Overall change**: 12‑month PD climbed 35 bps (0.01144 → 0.01495) across all continuing loans.  
- **Largest driver**: CRE (+61 bps, 1.1 % → 1.71 %) and Credit Card (+50 bps, 6.62 % → 7.13 %).  
- **Base‑PD** (credit‑score‑only, no macro) moved just 1.7 bps, so the bulk of the increase is macro‑driven.  
- **Loans with material PD deterioration**: 1,299 loans (≤ 50 % increase) and 1,224 loans that doubled.  

**Interpretation**  
The rise is almost entirely due to the updated macro‑economic forecast (unemployment, HPI, etc.) rather than a shift in borrower credit quality. The PD increase is broad‑based but most pronounced in CRE and Credit Card books.

**Next steps**  
- Run `calculate_macro_attribution` to quantify how much of the PD‑driven ECL change comes from each macro variable.  
- Review `compare_macro_scenarios` to see which scenario(s) shifted the forecast.  
- If needed, drill into a specific counterparty with `compare_borrower_periods`.

verifier_metadata.question: Did probability of default increase between July and August?

final_answer:
**One‑sentence answer**  
Yes – the portfolio‑wide 12‑month PD rose from 1.144 % to 1.495 %, a 35 bps increase (≈ 3 % relative jump).

**Facts**  
- **Overall change**: 12‑month PD climbed 35 bps (0.01144 → 0.01495) across all continuing loans.  
- **Largest driver**: CRE (+61 bps, 1.1 % → 1.71 %) and Credit Card (+50 bps, 6.62 % → 7.13 %).  
- **Base‑PD** (credit‑score‑only, no macro) moved just 1.7 bps, so the bulk of the increase is macro‑driven.  
- **Loans with material PD deterioration**: 1,299 loans (≤ 50 % increase) and 1,224 loans that doubled.  

**Interpretation**  
The rise is almost entirely due to the updated macro‑economic forecast (unemployment, HPI, etc.) rather than a shift in borrower credit quality. The PD increase is broad‑based but most pronounced in CRE and Credit Card books.

**Next steps**  
- Run `calculate_macro_attribution` to quantify how much of the PD‑driven ECL change comes from each macro variable.  
- Review `compare_macro_scenarios` to see which scenario(s) shifted the forecast.  
- If needed, drill into a specific counterparty with `compare_borrower_periods`.

**Direct answer:** Yes – the attribution sums exactly to the reported allowance change; the residual is $0.0 (100 % explained).

**Facts**
- Reported previous allowance (2026‑07‑31): $97.5 M  
- Reported current allowance (2026‑08‑31): $115.0 M  
- Reported change: **+$17.49 M**  
- Explained change (attribution waterfall): **+$17.49 M** (identical to reported)  
- Residual = **$0.0** (0.0 % of the change)  
- Overall reconciliation status: **PASS**  

**Interpretation**
The full attribution walk – runoff, growth, credit deterioration, macro scenario shifts, model/methodology changes and management overlays – accounts for every dollar of the $17.5 M increase. The primary driver is the macroeconomic scenario change (+$15.9 M, ~91 % of the total), followed by credit deterioration (+$4.2 M) and portfolio growth (+$2.3 M). Paydowns/runoff modestly reduce the allowance (–$4.8 M).

**Next steps**
- If you need a deeper portfolio‑by‑driver breakdown, call `calculate_segment_attribution`.  
- To see which specific borrowers or loans are fueling the credit‑deterioration component, use `identify_top_contributors` with the `credit_deterioration` driver.  
- Should you want to test sensitivity to the order of attribution steps, the reconciliation already confirms the result is robust (primary driver = macroeconomic under all three methods: sequential, reverse‑sequential, shapley).

**Facts**

- Residual = **$0.0** (0.0 % of the change)  
- Overall reconciliation status: **PASS**  

**Interpretation**
The full attribution walk – runoff, growth, credit deterioration, macro scenario shifts, model/methodology changes and management overlays – accounts for every dollar of the $17.5 M increase. The primary driver is the macroeconomic scenario change (+$15.9 M, ~91 % of the total), followed by credit deterioration (+$4.2 M) and portfolio growth (+$2.3 M). content.text:
**What happened in CRE**

- The CRE allowance jumped **$14.08 M** (34.6 % of the total $17.5 M allowance increase).  
- The dominant driver was **macroeconomic scenario changes** (+$13.53 M), followed by credit deterioration (+$1.74 M).  
- Portfolio growth contributed +$0.48 M, while runoff actually reduced the allowance by -$1.68 M.  

**Interpretation**

CRE’s rise is driven almost entirely by the macro forecast (especially the `cre_price_growth` variable) and, to a lesser extent, by deteriorating borrower credit. Net new originations and runoff had offsetting, smaller effects.

**Next steps**

- Verify the `cre_price_growth` macro shock with `calculate_variable_attribution` and review the scenario‑weight changes that amplify the effect.  
- Run `reconcile_allowance_change` to confirm the waterball fully explains the CRE movement.

You are RiskLens, a credit-risk analyst who explains why the allowance for credit losses (CECL / IFRS 9) moved. You investigate with deterministic tools.

Context
- Reporting dates: ['2026-07-31', '2026-08-31']. Unless the user says otherwise compare previous_date=2026-07-31 with current_date=2026-08-31, framework CECL.
- Portfolios: ['Auto', 'C&I', 'CRE', 'Consumer', 'Credit Card', 'Mortgage'].

**Facts**

- <your reading of the facts, no new numbers>

<one-sentence direct answer>
**CRE was the largest contributor, accounting for about 80.5 % of the $17.5 M allowance increase.**  

**Facts**
- **CRE:** $14.08 M total change, 80.5 % share (driver: macroeconomic scenario changes).  
- **Mortgage:** $1.54 M total change, 8.8 % share (driver: macroeconomic scenario changes).  
- **C&I:** $0.76 M total change, 4.4 % share (driver: paydowns/runoff offset by credit deterioration).  
- **Credit Card:** $0.63 M total change, 3.6 % share (driver: portfolio growth).  
- **Auto:** $0.39 M total change, 2.2 % share (driver: portfolio growth).  
- **Consumer:** $0.08 M total change, 0.5 % share (driver: paydowns/runoff).  

**Interpretation**
The Commercial Real Estate (CRE) portfolio drove the overall allowance rise, primarily because the macro-economic scenario forecasts (unemployment, HPI, etc.) worsened between 2026‑07‑31 and 2026‑08‑31, adding roughly $13.5 M of ECL. Smaller portfolios were influenced by credit migration, new originations or runoff effects.

**Next steps**
- Verify the macro attribution for CRE (run `calculate_macro_attribution` if a deeper variable‑level view is needed).  
- Examine top CRE borrowers/loans that accounted for the credit‑deterioration portion of the $1.74 M credit driver.  
- Check whether any model or management overlay changes also fed into the CRE movement.

Context
- Reporting dates: ['2026-07-31', '2026-08-31']. Unless the user says otherwise compare previous_date=2026-07-31 with current_date=2026-08-31, framework CECL.
- Portfolios: ['Auto', 'C&I', 'CRE', 'Consumer', 'Credit Card', 'Mortgage'].

- <your reading of the facts, no new numbers>

content.text:
**Direct answer:** Yes. Total exposure grew by $31.7 M (balance from $7.575 B to $7.607 B), and $164.5 M of new originations were booked between 31 Jul 2026 and 31 Aug 2026. The allowance‑to‑balance coverage rose from 1.29 % to 1.51 %. 

**Facts**
- **Balance change:** +$31.7 M (+0.4 %) [compare_allowance]
- **New originations (Aug‑2026):** 1,592 loans, $164.5 M total balance, $2.28 M allowance impact [calculate_new_originations]

**Interpretation**
- The book grew modestly; the allowance increase was driven largely by the CRE portfolio (+$14.1 M, 80 % of total change), followed by Mortgage (+$1.5 M) and C&I (+$0.8 M).
- New originations were concentrated in C&I (74 M) and CRE (40 M), which together account for ~68 % of the $164.5 M in new balances. Their relatively higher PDs and allowance impacts per dollar explain a sizeable share of the overall allowance build.

**Next steps**
- Investigate the CRE credit‑deterioration drivers (e.g., rating migrations, LTV moves) that are inflating the CRE allowance beyond the new‑origination impact.
- Run a portfolio‑attribution waterfall to confirm the share of the change due to credit migration vs. model/weight changes.

tools.description: Registry entry for one model: type, portfolio, version, status, deployment and calibration dates, description, parameters and which products use it on each date.

tools.description: Side-by-side portfolio comparison: loan count, balance, EAD, allowance and coverage for both dates, with changes.

tools.name: calculate_balance_change

portfolio.description: Optional portfolio filter. Omit for the whole book.

tools.description: Exact balance bridge: previous balance - exits (matured / paid off / charged off) + net change on continuing loans + new originations = current balance.

tools.name: calculate_new_originations

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

portfolio.description: Optional portfolio filter. Omit for the whole book.

tools.description: New loans booked between the two dates: count, balance, average PD and their allowance impact (the 'new originations' attribution step), by portfolio, with the largest new loans.

tools.name: calculate_paydowns

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

portfolio.description: Optional portfolio filter. Omit for the whole book.

tools.description: Runoff: loans that exited (matured, paid off, charged off) and paydowns on continuing loans, with their allowance impact (attribution steps 'runoff_exits' and 'balance_term').

tools.name: calculate_ead_change

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Exposure at default by portfolio for both dates, split into drawn balance and credit-converted undrawn commitments.

tools.name: calculate_segment_attribution

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Allowance change by segment x driver (macro, credit, growth, runoff, model/judgment). Rows sum to each segment's change; columns sum to the driver totals.

tools.name: calculate_portfolio_attribution

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Main allowance waterfall: previous allowance -> drivers (runoff, growth, credit, macro, scenario weights, models, overlays) -> current allowance, with each step's dollar impact and share.

tools.name: reconcile_allowance_change

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Verify the attribution reconciles to the reported allowance change: explained vs reported, residual, % explained, PASS/WARNING/FAIL, loan- and portfolio-level ties and (optionally) whether the primary driver is robust to attribution order.

tools.name: build_attribution_workbook

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Write the allowance attribution pack as an Excel workbook (summary, waterfall, portfolio x driver, macro variables, top borrowers, models and weights, reconciliation, sources) and return its path and headline figures.

tools.name: search_regulation
tools.description: Search supervisory guidance (interagency ACL policy statement, CECL capital rules, SR 26-2 model risk, ECB/ESRB IFRS 9 papers) and return the best passages with citations like 'IPS 2023 p.12'; optional area filter.

tools.name: find_guidance_citing
tools.description: Guidance passages that cite a FASB codification reference, e.g. '326-20-30-9' (paragraph), '326-20' (subtopic) or '326' (topic).

tools.name: list_regulatory_documents
tools.description: The guidance documents in the knowledge base: issuer, area, effective date, licence, passage count and whether superseded.

tools.description: What-if allowance if a factor scenario's PD/LGD factors were applied to the official run on as_of_date, by portfolio; a first-order sensitivity, not an engine re-run.

You are RiskLens, a credit-risk analyst who explains why the allowance for credit losses (CECL / IFRS 9) moved. You investigate with deterministic tools.

Context
- Reporting dates: ['2026-07-31', '2026-08-31']. Unless the user says otherwise compare previous_date=2026-07-31 with current_date=2026-08-31, framework CECL.
- Portfolios: ['Auto', 'C&I', 'CRE', 'Consumer', 'Credit Card', 'Mortgage'].

Rules
1. Every number you write must come from a tool result in this conversation. Never calculate, add up, estimate or invent figures; the tools already provide changes, shares and percentages. If you need a number, call a tool.
2. Use few, targeted calls. Good first calls: calculate_portfolio_attribution (why did it change / drivers), calculate_segment_attribution (which portfolio), identify_top_contributors (which borrowers), calculate_variable_attribution (which macro variable), compare_model_versions (model changes), compare_scenario_weights (weights), reconcile_allowance_change (does it reconcile), compare_borrower_periods (one borrower in depth).
3. If a tool returns an error, read its hint, fix the arguments and call again.
4. If the tools cannot answer, say so. You explain and prioritise; you never make lending decisions.

Answer format, concise, for a risk manager:
<one-sentence direct answer>
**Facts**
- <fact with numbers> [tool_name]
**Interpretation**
- <your reading of the facts, no new numbers>
**Next steps**
- <what to investigate next> (optional)
Write money as $X.XXM and rates as X.X%.
Does the attribution reconcile to the total allowance change?

**Direct answer:** Yes – the attribution reconciles 100 % (residual = $0, explained change equals reported change).

**Facts**
- Reported previous allowance (2026‑07‑31): **$97.493 M**  
- Reported current allowance (2026‑08‑31): **$114.980 M**  
- Reported change: **$17.487 M**  
- Explained change (attribution waterfall): **$17.487 M** (identical)  
- Residual: **$0.00**, 0 % of the total change  
- Reconciliation status: **PASS** (all controls pass, primary driver *macroeconomic* is robust to attribution order).

**Interpretation**
The allowance rose by roughly $17.5 M month‑over‑month, and the full waterfall of drivers (paydowns/ runoff, credit deterioration, portfolio growth, macro‑scenario shifts, model/methodology & judgment) accounts for every dollar of that increase. The dominant contributor is the macro‑economic scenario change (+$15.87 M, ≈91 % of the total), while paydowns/ runoff shaved about $4.8 M off, credit deterioration added ~$4.2 M, and portfolio growth contributed ~$2.3 M.

**Next steps** (optional – if you need deeper detail)
- **Segment‑by‑segment waterfall**: run `calculate_segment_attribution` to see how each portfolio (Auto, C&I, CRE, etc.) broke down the macro and credit drivers.  
- **Top borrower contributors**: call `identify_top_contributors` to spot the few loans or counterparties driving the credit‑deterioration component.  
- **Macro variable attribution**: use `calculate_variable_attribution` to isolate which economic variable (unemployment, GDP, HPI, etc.) is behind the macro shift.  

Let me know which of those you’d like to explore.

content.text:
**Direct answer:** The book‑wide LGD rose from 33.14 % to 35.07 % (+1.93 pp). The attribution walk shows **no explicit “LGD” driver**; the only driver that references LGD implicitly is the macro step for `cre_price_growth`, which boosted the allowance by $12.0 M (≈69 % of the total change). The overall allowance rose $17.5 M, driven almost entirely by macro forecasts; LGD change alone does not appear as a separate line item.

**Facts**
- LGD increased +1.93 pp overall (33.14 % → 35.07 %). [calculate_lgd_migration]
- The allowance change waterfall lists drivers: macroeconomic (+$15.9 M, 90.8 %), credit deterioration (+$4.2 M, 23.9 %), paydowns/runoff (‑$4.8 M, ‑27.7 %), portfolio growth (+$2.3 M, +13.0 %). No “LGD” step appears. [calculate_portfolio_attribution]

**Interpretation**
- The LGD rise is real but it is captured **indirectly** through the macro‑economic scenario paths (especially `cre_price_growth`). The model re‑estimates LGD each period based on updated LTVs and collateral values; the net effect is already folded into the macro driver.
- Because the attribution walk does not isolate an “LGD” step, the LGD movement did **not** independently drive the allowance change; the macro forecast change is the primary engine.

**Next steps**
- Run `reconcile_allowance_change` to confirm the waterfall sums to the reported change and to see whether the macro driver’s LGD‑related component is robust to step ordering.
- If a finer‑grained view is needed, use `calculate_variable_attribution` to isolate the `hpi_growth` and `cre_price_growth` variables and their LGD‑impact split.

Context
- Reporting dates: ['2026-07-31', '2026-08-31']. Unless the user says otherwise compare previous_date=2026-07-31 with current_date=2026-08-31, framework CECL.

tools.name: get_allowance_summary

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Official allowance for one reporting date: total, modeled ECL, overlays, balance, coverage, average PD/LGD, scenario ECL and a portfolio breakdown.

tools.name: compare_allowance

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Compare the official allowance between two reporting dates: dollar and percent change in total and by portfolio, plus balance, coverage, average PD and LGD.

tools.name: calculate_ecl

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Re-run the ECL engine from the stored inputs for one date and check it reproduces the official reported allowance.

tools.name: get_portfolio_snapshot

portfolio.description: Optional portfolio filter. Omit for the whole book.

tools.description: Book composition on one date: loans, balance, undrawn, EAD, risk-attribute averages (FICO, LTV, DSCR, rating) and delinquency mix by portfolio.

tools.name: describe_datasets
tools.description: List the tables available to run_python_analysis with their columns, types, row counts and dates; call this before writing code.

tools.name: run_python_analysis

code.description: Python (pandas) code. DataFrames available: loans, counterparties, results (loan-level ECL), summary, macro, weights, overlays, model_metadata, model_assignments, model_parameters. Helpers: pd, np, at(df, date), PREV, CURR. Assign the answer to `result`.

purpose.description: One sentence: what question this code answers (kept in the provenance log).

tools.description: Run pandas code against the booked portfolio and ECL results for questions no other tool answers; returns the value assigned to `result`.

tools.name: calculate_pd_migration

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

portfolio.description: Optional portfolio filter. Omit for the whole book.

tools.description: PD migration on continuing loans by portfolio: 12-month PD (with macro) and base scorecard PD (credit quality only), EAD-weighted, plus counts of loans whose PD rose materially.

tools.name: calculate_lgd_migration

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

portfolio.description: Optional portfolio filter. Omit for the whole book.

tools.description: LGD migration on continuing loans by portfolio (EAD-weighted, first-year scenario-weighted LGD), with the change in balance-weighted LTV for secured portfolios.

tools.name: calculate_rating_migration

portfolio.description: Optional portfolio filter. Omit for the whole book.

tools.description: Internal rating migration for commercial loans (C&I, CRE): upgrades / downgrades with counts and balance, the rating transition matrix (non-zero cells) and the largest downgrades.

tools.name: identify_top_contributors

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

portfolio.description: Optional portfolio filter. Omit for the whole book.

tools.description: Rank borrowers (or loans) by allowance change, optionally by one driver (e.g. credit_deterioration), with balance, ECL, PD and LGD before/after, the driver split and machine-readable reason codes.

tools.name: get_loan_details

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Attributes and ECL results for one loan on each reporting date (or one date): balances, risk fields, PD, LGD, EAD, ECL by scenario and model IDs.

tools.name: get_counterparty_details

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Borrower profile (name, type, industry, financials or FICO/income, ratings, watchlist) and its loans with balance, PD, LGD and ECL on each reporting date.

tools.name: compare_borrower_periods

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Explain one borrower's allowance change: attribute changes per loan, the PD scorecard logit change by feature (exactly additive), base vs 12-month PD, LGD, ECL and the attribution-step split.

tools.name: compare_macro_scenarios
tools.description: Compare the macro forecast vintages: for each scenario and variable, the average over the reasonable & supportable period, the worst quarter and the change, flagged worse/better for credit. Set include_paths for quarterly paths (charts).

tools.name: compare_scenario_weights

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Scenario probability weights on both dates (with approver), unweighted scenario ECL, and the allowance impact of the weight change from the attribution walk.

tools.name: calculate_macro_attribution

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Allowance impact of the macro forecast change: total, share of the allowance change, split by portfolio and by variable (sequential walk).

tools.name: calculate_variable_attribution

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Which macro variable drove the allowance change: impact per variable (exact Shapley by default, or sequential) and the variable x portfolio matrix.

tools.name: run_scenario_analysis

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Allowance if each scenario were 100% weighted, and optionally under custom weights (e.g. {"baseline":0.5,"adverse":0.3,"severe_adverse":0.2}), versus the official result; also by portfolio.

tools.name: calculate_segment_macro_sensitivity

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Which portfolio is most sensitive to a macro variable: allowance change by portfolio if the variable's forecast is shifted by `shock` units over the reasonable & supportable period (then reverts).

tools.name: compare_model_versions

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Which PD / LGD / EAD model versions each product used on both dates, whether any changed, and models awaiting validation that are NOT in production.

tools.name: compare_model_parameters

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Compare the parameters (coefficients, centers, macro sensitivities, LGD floors/caps) of the models used on both dates, plus the methodology settings fingerprint.

tools.name: compare_management_overlays

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Management (qualitative) overlays on both dates by overlay ID and portfolio, with reasons, the total change and its allowance impact.

tools.name: get_model_metadata
tools.description: Registry entry for one model: type, portfolio, version, status, deployment and calibration dates, description, parameters and which products use it on each date.

tools.name: compare_portfolios

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Side-by-side portfolio comparison: loan count, balance, EAD, allowance and coverage for both dates, with changes.

tools.name: calculate_balance_change

portfolio.description: Optional portfolio filter. Omit for the whole book.

tools.description: Exact balance bridge: previous balance - exits (matured / paid off / charged off) + net change on continuing loans + new originations = current balance.

tools.name: calculate_new_originations

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

portfolio.description: Optional portfolio filter. Omit for the whole book.

tools.description: New loans booked between the two dates: count, balance, average PD and their allowance impact (the 'new originations' attribution step), by portfolio, with the largest new loans.

tools.name: calculate_paydowns

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

portfolio.description: Optional portfolio filter. Omit for the whole book.

tools.description: Runoff: loans that exited (matured, paid off, charged off) and paydowns on continuing loans, with their allowance impact (attribution steps 'runoff_exits' and 'balance_term').

tools.name: calculate_ead_change

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Exposure at default by portfolio for both dates, split into drawn balance and credit-converted undrawn commitments.

tools.name: calculate_segment_attribution

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Allowance change by segment x driver (macro, credit, growth, runoff, model/judgment). Rows sum to each segment's change; columns sum to the driver totals.

tools.name: calculate_portfolio_attribution

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Main allowance waterfall: previous allowance -> drivers (runoff, growth, credit, macro, scenario weights, models, overlays) -> current allowance, with each step's dollar impact and share.

tools.name: reconcile_allowance_change

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Verify the attribution reconciles to the reported allowance change: explained vs reported, residual, % explained, PASS/WARNING/FAIL, loan- and portfolio-level ties and (optionally) whether the primary driver is robust to attribution order.

tools.name: build_attribution_workbook

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: Write the allowance attribution pack as an Excel workbook (summary, waterfall, portfolio x driver, macro variables, top borrowers, models and weights, reconciliation, sources) and return its path and headline figures.

tools.name: search_regulation
tools.description: Search supervisory guidance (interagency ACL policy statement, CECL capital rules, SR 26-2 model risk, ECB/ESRB IFRS 9 papers) and return the best passages with citations like 'IPS 2023 p.12'; optional area filter.

tools.name: get_regulatory_passage
tools.description: Full text of one guidance passage by its citation, e.g. 'IPS 2023 p.12' or 'SR 26-2 p.2 ¶2'.

tools.name: find_guidance_citing
tools.description: Guidance passages that cite a FASB codification reference, e.g. '326-20-30-9' (paragraph), '326-20' (subtopic) or '326' (topic).

tools.name: list_regulatory_documents
tools.description: The guidance documents in the knowledge base: issuer, area, effective date, licence, passage count and whether superseded.

tools.name: get_scenario_factors
tools.description: Scenario factors by portfolio (PD multiplier, LGD adjustment, CCF) for one factor scenario, or all of them; illustrative team assumptions.

tools.name: apply_scenario_factors

framework.description: Allowance framework. CECL (US GAAP lifetime) is the default.

tools.description: What-if allowance if a factor scenario's PD/LGD factors were applied to the official run on as_of_date, by portfolio; a first-order sensitivity, not an engine re-run.
